questions.q: A gp2 volume on a busy EC2 database is fast for a few days of heavy use, then I/O drops sharply and `BurstBalance` shows 0. The team wants predictable performance at low cost. What should they do?

options.t: Change the volume to gp3 with Elastic Volumes
options.why: Right: gp3 has no burst credits, a fixed baseline, and lets you set IOPS and throughput apart from size, at a lower price per GB than gp2.

options.t: Change the volume to sc1
options.why: Wrong: cold HDD is the slowest and cheapest class, and has its own burst credits.

options.t: Enable Fast Snapshot Restore on the volume
options.why: Wrong: FSR only removes lazy-load latency for volumes created from snapshots.

options.t: Turn on Multi-Attach
options.why: Wrong: it shares a volume between instances and does not fix throttling.

questions.explain: gp2 depends on burst credits; gp3 does not.
questions.remember: gp2, st1 and sc1 use burst credits (watch BurstBalance); gp3 and io2 do not. Slowdown after heavy use → move to gp3, or io2 for strict needs.
variants: Needs more than 80,000 IOPS or sub-millisecond latency → io2 Block Express.
Only the IOPS must grow, not the size → gp3 lets you raise IOPS alone.

questions.q: A self-managed Kafka cluster on EC2 stores large logs read sequentially. The team wants the lowest cost per MiB/s and does not need the volume to boot the OS. Which EBS type fits?

options.t: st1 throughput-optimized HDD
options.why: Right: built for big sequential reads such as logs, data warehouses and Kafka, and cheaper per MiB/s.

options.t: io2 Block Express
options.why: Wrong: top IOPS and sub-ms latency, but far more expensive than this workload needs.

options.t: sc1 cold HDD
options.why: Wrong: cheapest, but made for rarely accessed data with lower throughput.

options.t: gp2
options.why: Wrong: older SSD with IOPS tied to size; not the cheapest for sequential throughput.

questions.remember: Large sequential data (logs, Kafka, HDFS) on a budget → st1; rarely read and cheapest → sc1. HDD types cannot be boot volumes.
variants: The same disk must also be the boot volume → use an SSD type (gp3); st1 and sc1 cannot boot.
Small random I/O → SSD, not HDD.

questions.q: A compliance review finds an existing unencrypted EBS volume holding data. The company must encrypt it with a KMS key. What is the correct approach?

options.t: Enable encryption on the volume in place
options.why: Wrong: you cannot encrypt an existing unencrypted volume in place.

options.t: Snapshot it, copy the snapshot with encryption on, create a volume from the copy and swap it in
options.why: Right: encryption can only be added through a snapshot copy or a volume created from the snapshot with encryption.

options.t: Attach an encrypted volume to the same instance, which encrypts the first one
options.why: Wrong: mixing volumes on an instance does not change either one.

options.t: Change the KMS key on the volume to a customer managed key
options.why: Wrong: an unencrypted volume has no key, and an existing volume's key cannot be changed anyway.

questions.explain: Encrypt via snapshot copy, then swap volumes.
questions.remember: EBS encryption is set at creation. Encrypt an old volume via snapshot copy; to change a key, copy the snapshot with another key. Prevent the problem with encryption by default per Region.
variants: All future volumes must be encrypted → turn on EBS encryption by default in each Region.
Block creation of unencrypted volumes → IAM/SCP with the `ec2:Encrypted` condition key.
Detect unencrypted volumes → AWS Config rule `encrypted-volumes`.

questions.q: A team must share an encrypted EBS snapshot with another AWS account. The snapshot uses the default `aws/ebs` key and sharing fails. What fixes it?

options.t: Copy the snapshot, encrypting with a customer managed KMS key, then share the snapshot and allow the other account to use the key
options.why: Right: the AWS managed `aws/ebs` key cannot be shared; a customer managed key can, if the target account may use it.

options.t: Make the snapshot public
options.why: Wrong: public snapshots of encrypted volumes are not allowed.

options.t: Remove encryption from the snapshot first
options.why: Wrong: you cannot remove encryption from an encrypted snapshot.

options.t: Share only the key policy, not the snapshot
options.why: Wrong: the snapshot itself must also be shared.

questions.explain: Cross-account encrypted snapshots need a customer managed key.
questions.remember: Encrypted snapshot to another account → customer managed key, share the snapshot and grant key use. The default aws/ebs key cannot be shared.
variants: Share to another Region for DR → copy the snapshot cross-Region (can re-encrypt with another key).
Unencrypted snapshot → share directly with specific accounts.

questions.q: A volume created from a snapshot responds slowly on the first read of each block, which hurts a production launch. Which feature removes this latency at volume creation?

options.t: Fast Snapshot Restore on the snapshot in that AZ
options.why: Right: volumes from an FSR-enabled snapshot are fully initialized at creation, billed per snapshot per AZ per hour.

options.t: Snapshot Archive tier
options.why: Wrong: it makes storage cheaper and restores slower.

options.t: Recycle Bin
options.why: Wrong: it only keeps deleted snapshots for recovery.

options.t: Multi-Attach
options.why: Wrong: it shares a volume between instances and does not initialize blocks.

questions.explain: Lazy loading is fixed by FSR or by reading all blocks.
questions.remember: Slow first reads on a restored volume → lazy loading; use Fast Snapshot Restore (costs per hour per AZ) or initialize the blocks with fio/dd.
variants: No budget for FSR → initialize the volume by reading every block before production use.
A new empty volume → no pre-warming needed.

questions.q: Security wants protection from an admin deleting EBS snapshots by mistake and from ransomware that tries to delete backups. Choose TWO features.

options.t: Recycle Bin retention rules
options.why: Right: deleted snapshots (and AMIs) stay recoverable for the retention period.

options.t: Snapshot Lock
options.why: Right: makes snapshots immutable in governance or compliance mode.

options.t: Fast Snapshot Restore
options.why: Wrong: speeds up restores and does not protect snapshots.

options.t: Snapshot Archive tier
options.why: Wrong: it lowers cost for rarely restored snapshots and does not stop deletion.

options.t: Multi-Attach
options.why: Wrong: it is about sharing volumes between instances.

questions.explain: Recycle Bin for accidental deletes, Snapshot Lock for immutability.
questions.remember: Accidental deletion → Recycle Bin. Ransomware or compliance immutability → Snapshot Lock, plus cross-account copy.
variants: Scheduled snapshots with retention → Data Lifecycle Manager or AWS Backup.
Immutable backups across many services → AWS Backup Vault Lock.

questions.q: A Lambda function needs to read a 5 GB machine-learning model shared across many invocations. Which design works?

options.t: Mount an EFS file system through an access point, with the function configured in the VPC
options.why: Right: Lambda mounts EFS via an access point and needs VPC settings; good for big shared files and models.

options.t: Attach an EBS volume to the function
options.why: Wrong: Lambda cannot attach EBS volumes.

options.t: Mount EFS with no VPC configuration
options.why: Wrong: the function must be in the VPC to reach the mount target.

options.t: Put the model in the deployment package
options.why: Wrong: package size limits make a model this large unworkable.

questions.explain: Lambda mounts EFS via an access point inside a VPC.
questions.remember: Lambda + big shared files → EFS access point, function in the VPC with a security group allowing port 2049. Lambda cannot use EBS.
variants: Lambda cannot mount → check VPC config, security group, access point, and mount target in the function's AZ.
ECS or EKS needing shared persistent storage → EFS volumes (CSI driver on EKS).

questions.q: An EFS file system uses Bursting throughput. A spiky analytics job now stalls because `BurstCreditBalance` is 0. The team wants no capacity planning. What should they do?

options.t: Switch the file system to Elastic throughput
options.why: Right: Elastic scales throughput up and down automatically and you pay per data read or written.

options.t: Switch to Max I/O performance mode
options.why: Wrong: it is an older mode with higher latency and is unrelated to burst credits.

options.t: Add more mount targets in the same AZ
options.why: Wrong: only one mount target per AZ is allowed, and it does not add throughput.

options.t: Move to One Zone
options.why: Wrong: One Zone limits are not higher, and it lowers availability.

questions.explain: Out of burst credits and spiky load → Elastic.
questions.remember: Spiky or unpredictable throughput → Elastic (recommended default). Steady, known heavy throughput → Provisioned. Bursting scales with stored size and can run out of credits.
variants: Steady heavy known throughput → Provisioned (24-hour wait after changing).
Throughput should follow stored size and credits are enough → Bursting.

questions.q: EC2 instances in a new subnet hang when mounting an EFS file system. The file system exists and mount targets exist in other AZs. What are the likely causes? Choose TWO.

options.t: The mount target security group does not allow inbound TCP 2049 from the instances
options.why: Right: NFS uses port 2049 and the security group must allow it.

options.t: There is no mount target in the instances' AZ
options.why: Right: each AZ needs its own mount target, and the DNS name resolves to the one in the client's AZ.

options.t: The file system uses the Standard storage class
options.why: Wrong: storage class does not affect mounting.

options.t: EFS requires a public IP on the instance
options.why: Wrong: EFS has no public endpoint and is reached by private mount targets.

options.t: The instances need an EBS volume attached first
options.why: Wrong: EBS is unrelated to EFS mounting.

questions.explain: Check port 2049 and the mount target in that AZ.
questions.remember: EFS mount hangs → security group port 2049, mount target in the AZ, VPC DNS resolution. One mount target per AZ.
variants: Access denied after mounting → POSIX permissions, IAM ClientMount/ClientWrite, file system policy or access point.
Windows clients → EFS is Linux only; use FSx for Windows File Server.

questions.q: A company runs production on a Regional EFS file system and needs a disaster recovery copy in another Region, with a recovery point objective of about 15 minutes and no custom scripts. Which option fits?

options.t: EFS replication to a file system in the other Region
options.why: Right: continuous automatic copy of data and metadata, RPO typically 15 minutes; the destination is read-only until you delete the replication configuration.

options.t: Switch to One Zone storage
options.why: Wrong: One Zone keeps data in one AZ and lowers availability.

options.t: Mount the file system from the other Region over VPC peering
options.why: Wrong: this is not a copy, so a Region failure still takes the data away.

options.t: Copy files with a daily cron job on one EC2 instance
options.why: Wrong: a daily job gives an RPO of a day, not 15 minutes, and adds operations work.

questions.explain: Cross-Region DR for EFS is replication or AWS Backup copy.
questions.remember: EFS Region-level DR → replication (RPO about 15 minutes, read-only destination) or AWS Backup cross-Region copy. Regional EFS is already multi-AZ.
variants: Immutable backups needed → AWS Backup with vault lock.
The file system is One Zone → AZ loss loses it; use backups or replication.
Monitor lag → `TimeSinceLastSync`.

questions.q: A shared EFS file system holds project files. Most files are not touched for months, but some old files are occasionally opened again. How do you cut cost the most simply, keeping the file system shared across AZs?

options.t: Lifecycle management to IA and Archive, with move back to Standard on access
options.why: Right: files not accessed for N days move to cheaper classes, and hot files return to Standard when accessed.

options.t: Switch to One Zone
options.why: Wrong: it cuts price but loses multi-AZ availability, which the scenario still needs.

options.t: Copy old files to EBS
options.why: Wrong: EBS is single-instance block storage and not shared.

options.t: Set Provisioned throughput to the maximum
options.why: Wrong: it raises cost and does not reduce storage cost.

questions.explain: Cold data in EFS → lifecycle to IA or Archive.
questions.remember: EFS cost for cold data → lifecycle policy to IA/Archive (access fees apply), optionally back to Standard on access. Non-critical re-creatable data → One Zone classes.
variants: Data can be re-created and cost matters → One Zone classes.
Large cold data with API access → consider S3.

questions.q: A security team needs all EFS client connections to use encryption in transit, and clients mounted with plain NFS must be refused. What should they configure?

options.t: A file system policy that denies access when `aws:SecureTransport` is false, and mount with TLS using the EFS mount helper
options.why: Right: the resource-based policy enforces TLS and the mount helper (`-o tls`) or CSI driver supplies it.

options.t: Enable encryption at rest on the file system
options.why: Wrong: this protects stored data and does nothing for traffic.

options.t: Open port 2049 only to the VPC CIDR
options.why: Wrong: this limits who connects and does not require encryption.

options.t: Turn on EBS encryption by default
options.why: Wrong: EBS settings do not apply to EFS.

questions.explain: TLS is enforced by a file system policy plus a TLS mount.
questions.remember: Require TLS to EFS → file system policy deny on `aws:SecureTransport` false. Encryption at rest is set at creation and cannot be changed later.
variants: Unencrypted file system must be encrypted → create a new one and copy data (DataSync).
Need per-app user and root directory → access point.
Require IAM authorization for clients → mount option `iam` and ClientMount/ClientWrite.
